summary:
Ares Through Eons is a colony-management roguelike that puts young players in charge of making Mars livable. No single mission can do it, so players lead a series of expeditions across eras (“eons”). Each one lands a crew, builds a base, and researches new technology before it must evacuate, and the next era returns to the same site with better tools and higher stakes.

Players build real mission hardware, from habitats and greenhouses to a fission power plant, and unlock it through a research tree in which every project teaches a fact from a real NASA mission. The map is real Martian terrain from NASA Mars Trek, and radiation storms are driven by NASA space weather data.

By keeping a crew fed, powered, and safe, players learn why Mars is hard, and why exploration is built step by step over many missions, the way NASA’s own plans are.
details:
What it does
Ares Through Eons is a browser game where the player leads a crew of four astronauts on Mars. Each crew member has a job (engineer, scout, researcher, or medic) and needs oxygen, water, food, and rest. The player places modules such as a habitat, research lab, greenhouse, med bay, and power plant, links them with tubes, and manages oxygen, water, food, power, ice, and regolith. Radiation storms force the crew to shelter. When an era ends, the expedition evacuates, and the next one returns to the same site with new technology, while the old landers and buildings remain, worn down by Mars.

Benefits and intended impact
The game teaches by doing. Every research project is written in plain language for young players and links to the real NASA mission behind it, such as MOXIE making oxygen from Martian air or Kilopower testing a small reactor. Players learn why water ice, radiation shielding, and power matter because their crew depends on them. Our aim is for players to come away understanding that reaching Mars is a long chain of missions, each building on the last.

Tools and technology
The project is entirely software. It is written in TypeScript with React and Vite. The map is drawn with PixiJS (using @pixi/react, pixi-viewport and @pixi/sound), and the rotating Mars globe on the main menu uses Three.js. Game state is managed with Zustand, the interface uses Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui and Lucide React icons, and the game is hosted on Vercel. Sprites were modelled in Blender and cut into pixel-art layers.

How it is creative
The landing site is real Martian terrain, built from NASA Mars Trek imagery and elevation data and drawn as pixel art. Space weather in the game is driven by NASA data. Buildings and astronauts are “sprite stacks”: simple 3D models sliced into thin layers so they look solid from the game’s tilted view. The four spaceships follow the Artemis missions.

What we considered
We designed for readability at a young age, using chunky shapes and a small shared colour palette. We describe modules as “based on” NASA concepts, since NASA has no single official Mars base design. The med bay uses a white plus, not a red cross, which is a protected emblem. The astronauts are gender neutral and come in several complexions.
